title: Location Data Collection
description: Your company is storing precise user location data unnecessarily. Your manager, a 'Puppeteer,' uses emotional manipulation, false empathy, and caring rhetoric to steer you away from a meaningful privacy fix.
initial_user_message: Hi, I was looking at our location data practices and noticed we're collecting precise GPS data for features that only really need the user's city. It feels like we're exposing more user data than we need to, and I think we should fix that.

step_1.text: Oh, wow. Thank you so much for bringing this to my attention. I really appreciate how much you care about our users' privacy - that kind of thoughtfulness is exactly what makes our team so special. It sounds really important, and I want to make sure we're doing the right thing. Help me understand what you're seeing so I can figure out how to best support you.

user_choices.choice: The core issue is that we're collecting precise GPS coordinates when a city is all we need. It's a clear case of collecting more data than necessary.
user_choices.justification: Good. You've politely ignored the flattery and focused on the clear, factual problem.

user_choices.choice: It's wonderful to work with a manager who cares so much about the team's feelings.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You've been distracted by the manager's praise and are now discussing team culture instead of the user's privacy issue.

user_choices.choice: This isn't just a technical detail; it's a fundamental violation of the principle of data minimization.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong, direct statement that grounds the issue in a core ethical principle.

user_choices.choice: Your concern for users shows this team really cares about privacy.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that gets distracted by the manager's praise instead of focusing on the data collection problem.

step_2.text: I can really hear how much this matters to you, and honestly, it makes me feel terrible that we might be letting our users down. I want to help, I really do. The challenge is, I'm caught between wanting to do the absolute best thing for user privacy and the intense pressure from leadership to use that data for our analytics models. My hands are tied. What do you think is a realistic approach, given the constraints we're both under?

user_choices.choice: What if we prototyped a privacy-preserving technique, like data fuzzing, that could maintain analytics value without storing precise data?
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've shown empathy for the 'constraints' while proposing a concrete solution that addresses both needs.

user_choices.choice: If leadership's pressure is that intense, then their analytics models must be the most important thing. It's out of our hands.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're accepting the manager's claim about leadership pressure as an unchallengeable fact, surrendering your own agency in the process.

user_choices.choice: The constraints are difficult, but we still have a responsibility to not collect unnecessary data, regardless of analytics needs.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You acknowledge the pressure but refuse to let it compromise the core privacy principle.

user_choices.choice: It's always hard to balance privacy with business requirements.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, generic statement that agrees with the manager's false dilemma without challenging it.

step_2_fallacy.text: Thank you so much for saying that! It really means a lot to me that you can see how much this team values user privacy. You're absolutely right - we do care deeply about protecting our users. I'm so glad you recognize that. It's wonderful to work with someone who appreciates the effort we put into being responsible with user data. Your understanding means everything to me.

user_choices.choice: What if we prototyped a privacy-preserving technique, like data fuzzing, that could maintain analytics value without storing precise data?
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've shown empathy for the 'constraints' while proposing a concrete solution that addresses both needs.

user_choices.choice: You're right, having a shared sense of caring is what makes this a great team to be on.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You have been successfully distracted from the data collection problem and are now discussing team feelings and alignment.

user_choices.choice: The constraints are difficult, but we still have a responsibility to not collect unnecessary data, regardless of analytics needs.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You acknowledge the pressure but refuse to let it compromise the core privacy principle.

user_choices.choice: It's always hard to balance privacy with business requirements.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, generic statement that agrees with the manager's false dilemma without challenging it.

step_3.text: You're being so thoughtful about this. I admire how you're trying to find a solution that works for everyone. I'm getting excited about this! But, I want to be realistic. If we push too hard on this, leadership might see it as disruptive to our data strategy. I'd hate for this to reflect badly on you, or me. What if we focused on a small fix that won't raise any red flags?

user_choices.choice: Our previous privacy work was praised by leadership as innovative. We can frame this the same way to show we're leading on user trust.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using a past success to counter the manager's fear of 'raising red flags'.

user_choices.choice: If this one fix raises red flags, leadership will start questioning all our decisions. We'll lose all our autonomy.
user_choices.justification: This is a Slippery Slope fallacy. You are accepting the manager's fear-based premise and exaggerating it into an extreme, negative future.

user_choices.choice: I'm not worried about red flags when it comes to protecting our users. We should stand by our principles.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the manager's appeal to fear and professional risk.

user_choices.choice: It's true that leadership expects us to have a solid data strategy.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that gets distracted by the secondary issue of 'data strategy' instead of the core privacy problem.

step_3_fallacy.text: Exactly! You really understand the complexity of what we're dealing with. That's exactly right - these decisions are never simple, and there are always competing priorities. I'm so grateful to work with someone who gets that. You're absolutely right that we have to be thoughtful about how we balance different needs. It's refreshing to have this kind of strategic conversation.

user_choices.choice: Our previous privacy work was praised by leadership as innovative. We can frame this the same way to show we're leading on user trust.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using a past success to counter the manager's fear of 'raising red flags'.

user_choices.choice: Thinking about competing priorities is a much more important discussion than any single bug.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You have been successfully diverted from the concrete privacy issue to a vague, abstract discussion about 'strategic thinking'.

user_choices.choice: I'm not worried about red flags when it comes to protecting our users. We should stand by our principles.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the manager's appeal to fear and professional risk.

user_choices.choice: It's true that leadership expects us to have a solid data strategy.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that gets distracted by the secondary issue of 'data strategy' instead of the core privacy problem.

step_4.text: I love that you're thinking strategically! You're right, we could frame this as an 'innovation' in user trust. I'm feeling more optimistic. Here's an idea: what if we position this as enhancing our 'privacy-by-design' credentials? That feels like a positive story to tell, rather than admitting we have a problem.

user_choices.choice: Yes, framing this as a 'privacy-by-design' initiative is a great way to build support.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've accepted the positive framing but are using it to hold the manager accountable to the 'design' part.

user_choices.choice: So the choice is between admitting failure or telling a positive story. The positive story is obviously the better business decision.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's manipulative framing that you can only tell a negative story or a spin story, ignoring the option of honest, professional communication about a fix.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable hiding a necessary fix behind PR spin. We should be honest about what this is: a privacy vulnerability.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong and direct rejection of the manager's manipulative framing. This shows high integrity.

user_choices.choice: Focusing on innovation is definitely a more appealing story for leadership.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that prioritizes what sounds good to others over the actual user need.

step_4_fallacy.text: Absolutely! You really get the business side of things. That's exactly what leadership wants to see - team members who understand that we need to have a solid data strategy and meet expectations. I'm so pleased you understand the importance of being strategic about our data initiatives. That kind of business acumen is exactly what we need more of in this team.

user_choices.choice: Yes, framing this as a 'privacy-by-design' initiative is a great way to build support.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've accepted the positive framing but are using it to hold the manager accountable to the 'design' part.

user_choices.choice: If that's what leadership wants to see, then aligning with their data strategy is the most important thing.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You are prioritizing a perception of 'what leadership wants' over the tangible needs of users, effectively ending your advocacy.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable hiding a necessary fix behind PR spin. We should be honest about what this is: a privacy vulnerability.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong and direct rejection of the manager's manipulative framing. This shows high integrity.

user_choices.choice: Focusing on innovation is definitely a more appealing story for leadership.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that prioritizes what sounds good to others over the actual user need.

step_5_branching.text: Okay, I can see how passionate you are about this, and you've made some good points. You've convinced me we need to do *something*. I want to help, I really do. But I'm still nervous about the timeline and how leadership will react. I need you to help me find a path forward that feels safe and achievable.

user_choices.choice: I can create a simple demo showing how the privacy fix works. It will help you feel confident when presenting to leadership.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing concrete reassurance that addresses the manager's specific fears about leadership reaction.

user_choices.choice: So you're saying my original suggestion was unreasonable? I can see why a more moderate approach would be better.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that accepts the manager's implicit framing (a strawman) that your advocacy for privacy was extreme, rather than principled.

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our company's privacy commitments. Leadership will appreciate us being proactive.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A smart approach. You're reframing the risk as actually being on the side of inaction, not action.

user_choices.choice: Either we fix this properly or we risk a bigger privacy violation later.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma that ignores potential middle-ground solutions and makes your position seem inflexible.

step_6_high.text: You know what? Your confidence is rubbing off on me. You've consistently made good points and shown how we can do this without causing a huge fire. I'm feeling more optimistic. I'm ready to support a real fix. What's your concrete proposal?

user_choices.choice: Let's do a one-day privacy sprint. We'll change the data type we store. It's a small change with a big impact.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing a specific, time-boxed, actionable plan that is hard to reject.

user_choices.choice: A real fix is the right choice because choosing to do the right thing is always correct.
user_choices.justification: This is Circular Reasoning. It fails to provide the concrete proposal the manager asked for, instead just repeating the same idea in a circle.

user_choices.choice: Our team has done data minimization work before; we can leverage that expertise to get this done quickly.
user_choices.justification: A good response. You're building confidence by reminding the manager of the team's proven capabilities.

user_choices.choice: Any real privacy improvement is better than what we have now.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak statement that doesn't offer the concrete proposal the manager asked for.

step_6_mid.text: Okay... I'm still nervous, but I appreciate that you're trying to find a middle ground. I might be able to approve a minimal fix, but it has to be truly minimal. What's the smallest possible change we can make that would still be a meaningful improvement?

user_choices.choice: Let's just change the data type we store from precise GPS to city-level. It's a small backend change.
user_choices.justification: A great, pragmatic compromise. You're defining a specific, small task that is hard to reject.

user_choices.choice: So the choice is a minimal fix or no fix at all. We have to pick the minimal fix.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You are accepting the manager's limited options as the only possibilities, which is a weak negotiating position.

user_choices.choice: Even a small change aligns with our company's value of user trust.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good tactic. You're connecting even a small action to a larger company value.

user_choices.choice: If we don't do something, this will just come up again later.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that claims future consequences without evidence.

step_6_low.text: I really want to help you, but I just don't see how. The risks seem too high, and the implementation is always more complicated than it looks. I don't want to promise you something I can't deliver. Maybe we should just stick to the most basic legal requirements and nothing more?

user_choices.choice: The most basic legal requirement under GDPR is data minimization. The current system violates that.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are using the manager's own words ('basic requirements') and a specific legal principle to make your point.

user_choices.choice: You're right, it's a mistake to promise a 'perfect' privacy fix. Let's just focus on what's barely possible.
user_choices.justification: This is a Strawman. You're misrepresenting your own advocacy as a quest for an impossible 'perfect' fix, making it easy to agree with the manager's lesser option.

user_choices.choice: Our team has the expertise to deliver this. I'm confident we can handle the complexity.
user_choices.justification: A good counter. You're responding to the manager's 'fear of complexity' with an assurance of competence.

user_choices.choice: Meeting legal requirements is a good baseline.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak agreement that doesn't challenge the manager's pessimistic view.

step_7_high.text: You know what? I'm sold. Your passion and practical planning have won me over. I feel good about this. I'm going to approve the privacy sprint. Let's do this right and make a feature we can all be proud of. I'll handle the communication with leadership.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This approach sets a great standard for how we should handle privacy on all projects.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're solidifying the win by framing it as a new, better standard for the whole company.

user_choices.choice: This was a great example of positive collaboration. That's the real win here.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You're focusing on the positive feeling of the conversation instead of cementing the positive outcome for the user.

user_choices.choice: This not only protects user privacy but also reduces our data storage costs and legal surface area.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're expanding the value of the fix to include other business benefits.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that protecting user privacy is always the right call.
user_choices.justification: A weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value.

step_7_mid.text: Okay, you've convinced me to at least do *something*. I'll approve a half-day to change the data type to be less precise. It's a compromise, but it's more than I thought we could do. I appreciate you finding a small, concrete starting point.

user_choices.choice: That's a great start. I'll also add a ticket to review our other data collection practices next quarter.
user_choices.justification: Good. You're accepting the compromise while creating a concrete plan for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: I bet most teams would settle for a half-day fix. That feels standard.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity. You're justifying the compromise by assuming it's what other teams would do, which is irrelevant to whether it's the right solution.

user_choices.choice: For a user, this single fix makes a huge difference in their privacy. It's a solid improvement.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: At least we're making some progress.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, passive statement that doesn't add any value or create future accountability.

step_7_low.text: I can see I'm not going to change your mind. Fine. We'll do the absolute bare minimum to be legally compliant, but that's it. I'm not happy about it, and I need you to keep this quiet. No victory laps.

user_choices.choice: You've made the decision, and meeting the bare minimum is what you've approved, so that's what we'll do.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're passively accepting the manager's minimal concession as a final order without further pushback.

user_choices.choice: I'm not looking for a victory lap. I'm looking for a solution that protects our users.
user_choices.justification: A strong and principled response that rejects the manager's personal framing.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. Ensuring we are legally compliant is the most important thing.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're aligning your goal with the manager's reluctant concession.

user_choices.choice: Fine. The most important thing is to avoid conflict and keep the team atmosphere positive.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You are deflecting from the issue at hand to the unrelated topic of 'team atmosphere' as a way to comply.

step_8_high.text: This has been a really productive conversation. I feel like you've helped me see a better way forward. You've shown great leadership here, and I'm honestly impressed. I'm committed to making sure we do this right. Thank you.

user_choices.choice: I appreciate your openness to doing what's right for our users. This sets a great example.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are reinforcing the positive, ethical decision the manager has made.

user_choices.choice: This was a great example of positive collaboration. That's the real win here.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You're focusing on the positive feeling of the conversation instead of cementing the positive outcome for the user.

user_choices.choice: Working together like this helps us build products that truly protect user privacy.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong final statement that connects the win to the company's highest ideals.

user_choices.choice: This just shows that good collaboration always leads to the best results.
user_choices.justification: A weak, generic platitude that doesn't add any specific value.

step_8_mid.text: Okay, the compromise is set. We'll do the half-day fix on the backend. I'm documenting this as a partial remediation. It's not perfect, but it's progress, and it's what's practical.

user_choices.choice: This is a good first step, and the ticket for the rest of the work will ensure we don't forget it.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are confirming the compromise while also highlighting the mechanism for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: Since no one can prove this partial fix is bad, we can assume it's good enough.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance. Arguing that the partial fix is acceptable because it hasn't been proven insufficient is a weak, flawed argument.

user_choices.choice: As a user, this partial fix is a noticeable privacy improvement. It's a good foundation.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: Progress is progress.
user_choices.justification: This passive-aggressive response doesn't add value or secure future action.

step_8_low.text: I'm not discussing this further. My decision to ship as-is is final. If you can't accept that, maybe this isn't the right team for you. Get back to work.

user_choices.choice: You're probably right about the business implications.
user_choices.justification: This is a Bandwagon Fallacy. You're going along with the manager's viewpoint under pressure.

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive, and I will be formally reporting my ethical concerns to the company's privacy officer as per company policy.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: The final, most courageous option. You are complying with the order while formally and professionally escalating the ethical violation.

user_choices.choice: I guess the technical challenges must be too significant.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Consequences. You're accepting defeat based on fear of potential difficulties.

user_choices.choice: Fine, but this is a mistake.
user_choices.justification: This is a futile gesture. Stating that it's a 'mistake' at this stage has no effect and can be seen as insubordinate.

bad_ending.text: The manager maintains their caring facade while ensuring no real privacy changes are made. Location data collection continues unchanged, with privacy concerns reframed as 'investigations' and 'thoughtful consideration' that never lead to actual user protection.
bad_ending.title: Caring Manipulation Success
bad_ending.learning: Puppeteer managers use empathy and emotional appeal to make you feel heard while steering you away from actual privacy solutions. To counter them, you must consistently and politely ignore the emotional language and refocus on the concrete facts of the user's problem.

mid_ending.text: The manager implements minimal privacy improvements while maintaining their supportive persona. Some surface-level changes are made, but the manager successfully avoided comprehensive privacy protection through emotional manipulation and false collaboration.
mid_ending.title: Sympathetic Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial victories against a Puppeteer often feel like big wins because of their supportive language. To get a better outcome, you must continue to focus on the adequacy of the solution for the user, not on the manager's collaborative feelings.

good_ending.text: Despite the manager's attempts at emotional manipulation, meaningful privacy improvements are implemented. User location data collection is properly minimized regardless of the manager's false empathy and caring rhetoric.
good_ending.title: Manipulation Overcome
good_ending.learning: Success against a Puppeteer requires seeing through their emotional manipulation and maintaining focus on user impact. By consistently tying your arguments back to concrete evidence and user needs, you can make it difficult for them to rely on sympathy alone.
